pathway.title: Programming
pathway.description: Learn to write clear, working programs by progressing from instructions and values to Python functions, collections, and a small text-based program.

course.title: Python Programming — Beginner
course.short_description: A complete first course in Python programming. Learners build accurate foundations with values, text, decisions, loops, lists, functions, dictionaries, and safe error handling.
course.prerequisites: No programming experience required. Learners should be able to read simple instructions and use a school-approved device that can run Python 3.10 or newer.
learning_outcomes: Describe a task as inputs, processing steps, and outputs before coding.
Write and run short Python scripts using variables, built-in types, arithmetic, and text.
Use conditions and loops to make a program choose and repeat instructions.
Organize related information with lists and dictionaries and reuse work with functions.
Handle common conversion errors, test representative cases, and explain a small program.
course.dependencies: Python 3.10+ standard library only; no third-party packages required.

modules.title: Start with Python and clear instructions
modules.description: Think in algorithms, run a short Python script, and store values with clear names and types.

topics.title: Think in clear steps: algorithms and instructions
topics.description: A computer follows instructions; it does not guess what a person meant.

lesson.title: Think in clear steps: algorithms and instructions
objectives: Explain what a program and an algorithm are in your own words.
Break a familiar task into ordered, unambiguous steps.
Identify an input, a process, and an output in a simple problem.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A computer follows instructions; it does not guess what a person meant. A program is a set of instructions written in a language a computer can run. Before writing code, programmers can describe an algorithm: a finite, ordered set of steps that solves a problem. Start by naming the information available (input), the work to do (process), and the result wanted (output). For example, to work out the total cost of two items, the inputs are the two prices, the process is addition, and the output is the total. Clear steps avoid hidden assumptions. “Get ready” is vague; “put the book in your bag” is more precise. Algorithms can be written as numbered steps, a flow diagram, or pseudocode. Python will later express those ideas with exact syntax. For this course, focus first on reasoning about the task, not on memorising code.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
first_price = 120
second_price = 80
total = first_price + second_price
print(total)
blocks.explanation: The two prices are inputs stored in names. The plus sign performs the process, and `print` displays the output. The numbers are practice values in the same units; the program does not know whether they represent shillings or something else unless we label them for a person.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A three-part sequence showing two input prices flowing to an addition process and then to the total 200.
blocks.content: Input: 120 and 80  →  Process: add the values  →  Output: 200

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Write numbered steps for a program that asks for the length and width of a rectangle and displays its area. Label the two inputs, the calculation, and the output before trying to code it.
success_checks: The steps name both measurements as inputs.
The process multiplies length by width.
The final step clearly displays the area.

items.prompt: Which order best describes a simple input-process-output algorithm?
Why should an algorithm use unambiguous steps?

choices.text: So the computer can guess the missing details
So different readers can follow the same intended procedure
So every program uses the same number of lines
So Python syntax is no longer needed

items.prompt: In a recipe-like algorithm that adds two prices, what is the process?

revision_notes: An algorithm is a finite, ordered procedure.
Identify input, process, and output before coding.
Computers follow explicit instructions rather than guessing intent.

topics.title: Run a Python script and display output
topics.description: Python is a programming language whose interpreter reads and runs instructions.

lesson.title: Run a Python script and display output
objectives: Distinguish Python code from the text printed by a program.
Use `print()` to display text and simple values.
Recognise comments and a basic syntax error in a short script.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Python is a programming language whose interpreter reads and runs instructions. A script is a text file containing Python code; a Python shell can also run one instruction at a time. The exact launch steps vary by device, so use the Python environment approved by your school or device administrator. In this course, examples use Python 3.10 or newer and no extra packages. The built-in `print()` function sends a value to the output area. Text needs matching quotation marks; `print(2 + 3)` calculates first and displays 5. A comment begins with `#` and helps a human understand the code; Python ignores the remainder of that line. Syntax means the language's spelling and structure rules. A missing quote or parenthesis can stop the script before it runs. Read the first error line and the indicated line number carefully. Small scripts are easier to inspect when each instruction has a clear purpose.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The first line is a comment, not an instruction. The first `print` displays the characters inside quotes. The second evaluates the arithmetic expression before displaying its result. The source code and the output are related, but they are not the same thing.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A source file is read by the Python interpreter, which either displays output or reports an error to inspect.
blocks.content: Python source file  →  Python interpreter  →  output or an error message

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Create a three-line greeting script: add one comment, print a greeting, and print the result of 7 + 5. Run it in an approved Python 3 environment. Then remove a closing parenthesis and observe how the error points to the problem.
success_checks: The comment begins with `#` and does not print.
The greeting appears as text, and the calculation appears as 12.
The learner can locate and repair the missing parenthesis.

items.prompt: What does `print(2 + 3)` display?
What does a `#` begin on a normal Python code line?
If a quote is missing, what is a useful first response?

choices.text: Read the syntax error and inspect the indicated line

revision_notes: A script is Python source saved as text; the interpreter runs it.
`print()` displays a value, while `#` starts a comment.
Treat an error message as information and inspect its line reference.

topics.title: Store values with variables and basic types
topics.description: A variable is a name that refers to a value.

lesson.title: Store values with variables and basic types
objectives: Create descriptive variables using Python assignment syntax.
Recognise integer, decimal, text, and Boolean values.
Explain why a variable's value can change during a program.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A variable is a name that refers to a value. In `books_count = 4`, the equals sign assigns the value 4 to the name `books_count`; it is not the same as an equality test. Descriptive names help a reader understand what a value represents. Python distinguishes types: integers such as 4, decimal numbers such as 4.5 (called `float`), text in quotes such as `"Python"` (called `str`), and the truth values `True` and `False` (called `bool`). A type affects which operations make sense. Adding two integers performs arithmetic, while adding two strings joins text. Reassigning a variable gives its name a new value: after `score = score + 1`, the updated score is used in later instructions. Use lowercase words with underscores for multiword names, and avoid names that hide their meaning. In the Python shell, `type(value)` can help you inspect a value's type.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
book_title = "Mti wa Hadithi"
books_count = 4
price = 250.0
is_available = True
print(type(books_count).__name__)
print(book_title)
blocks.explanation: `book_title` refers to text, `books_count` to an integer, `price` to a float, and `is_available` to a Boolean. The `type(...).__name__` expression displays a readable type name. The example stores no information about a real learner or borrower.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A variable name refers to a value, and each value has a type such as int, float, str, or bool.
blocks.content: name  →  value  →  type (for example, books_count → 4 → int)

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Create four variables for a fictional reading list: a book title, number of pages, average rating, and whether the book is available. Print each value and predict its type before checking with `type()`.
success_checks: Text is surrounded by matching quotes.
The count is an integer and the rating is a decimal number.
Availability is written as `True` or `False`, with capital first letters.

items.prompt: What is the type of the value `3.0`?
Which is a valid descriptive variable name?
What does `available = False` assign to the name `available`?

revision_notes: Assignment uses `name = value`; later assignments can update the value.
Common beginner types are `int`, `float`, `str`, and `bool`.
Choose readable names that communicate what a value represents.

modules.title: Use data, text, and decisions
modules.description: Calculate with numbers, work with text, and select a branch with comparisons and conditions.

topics.title: Calculate with numbers and convert input
topics.description: Python's arithmetic operators include `+` for addition, `-` for subtraction, `*` for multiplication, `/` for division, and `//` for floor division, which rounds a quotient down toward negative infinity (integer operands produce an integer result).

lesson.title: Calculate with numbers and convert input
objectives: Use arithmetic operators to calculate a total or average.
Explain operator precedence in a short expression.
Convert numeric text to an integer or float before arithmetic.
Use the remainder operator `%` to identify an even integer.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Python's arithmetic operators include `+` for addition, `-` for subtraction, `*` for multiplication, `/` for division, and `//` for floor division, which rounds a quotient down toward negative infinity (integer operands produce an integer result). The `%` operator returns the remainder, so `8 % 2` is 0 and `7 % 2` is 1; this is useful for testing whether a whole number is even. Parentheses make the intended order clear; multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction when there are no parentheses. The built-in `input()` function always returns text, even when a person types digits. To calculate with a whole number, convert that returned text with `int()`; for a decimal, use `float()`. A conversion fails if the text is not a valid number, so later you will learn how to handle that safely. Store intermediate values with descriptive names instead of packing every operation into one long expression. When a calculation has a real-world meaning, state its units to the reader. These arithmetic examples use simple practice values and do not involve money movement or financial records.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
first = int(input("First whole number: "))
second = int(input("Second whole number: "))
total = first + second
print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"8 % 2 = {8 % 2}")
print(f"7 % 2 = {7 % 2}")
blocks.explanation: Each `input()` result is text, so `int()` converts it before addition. The f-string displays the total. The `%` operator returns a remainder: a whole number is even when dividing it by 2 leaves remainder 0, while 7 leaves remainder 1. If the learner types a word instead of digits, `int()` raises an error; input validation is introduced later in the course.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: Typed digits first arrive as text, are converted to an integer, used in a calculation, and then displayed.
blocks.content: typed characters  →  input() text  →  int() conversion  →  arithmetic  →  displayed result

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Write a script that asks for two whole-number practice values, converts both with `int()`, calculates their sum and displays it. Use `% 2` to decide whether the first value is even. Try 12 and 8, then run again with 13 as the first value and explain why the results differ.
success_checks: Both values are converted before addition.
The example inputs produce a total of 20.
The remainder check identifies 12 as even and 13 as odd.

items.prompt: What type of value does `input()` return?
Which condition checks whether an integer `number` is even?
Which conversion is suitable for the text `"7"` when a whole-number calculation is needed?

revision_notes: Use arithmetic operators for calculations; `%` returns a remainder and `//` performs floor division.
`input()` gives text; convert with `int()` or `float()` before numeric work.
Use parentheses and named intermediate values to make calculations readable.

topics.title: Work with text, input, and formatted messages
topics.description: Text in Python is a string (`str`).

lesson.title: Work with text, input, and formatted messages
objectives: Create string values and join them safely into a message.
Use `strip()` and `lower()` to prepare text for comparison.
Build a readable output with an f-string.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Text in Python is a string (`str`). Strings can hold names of objects, short labels, and messages. `input()` is useful for asking a question, but its result is text; a number typed at the keyboard is still a string until converted. An f-string begins with the letter `f` before its opening quote and lets an expression inside braces be inserted into a message. For example, `f"Habari, {name}!"` produces a greeting using the current value of `name`. Text methods can help normalize a value: `.strip()` removes spaces at the beginning and end, while `.lower()` creates a lowercase version. These methods return a new string; they do not silently change the original value. Comparing normalized text can make a search less sensitive to extra spaces or letter case. Always show a clear prompt and avoid asking a learner to enter private personal information for a practice program.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
title = input("Book title: ").strip()
print(f"You entered: {title}")
print(title.lower())
blocks.expected_output:
You entered: Mti wa Hadithi
mti wa hadithi
blocks.explanation: `strip()` removes the extra outer spaces before assignment. The f-string inserts the cleaned title. `lower()` returns a lowercase copy for the final display, but `title` itself keeps its original capitalization.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: Entered text can be trimmed, then inserted in a message or normalized for comparison.
blocks.content: raw text  →  strip() cleanup  →  f-string message or normalized comparison

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Ask for a fictional book title. Store the cleaned text with `strip()`, print it in an f-string, and display a lowercase version for search. Try input with extra spaces and mixed capital letters.
success_checks: Outer spaces do not remain in the stored title.
The output message includes the entered title.
The lowercase search form does not overwrite the display form.

items.prompt: What does `"  Python  ".strip()` return?
Which syntax inserts `name` into a message?
What is the main effect of `text.lower()`?

choices.text: It converts text to an integer

revision_notes: Text is represented by the `str` type.
Use f-strings to insert values into clear output messages.
`strip()` trims outer whitespace and `lower()` helps normalize comparisons.

topics.title: Make decisions with comparisons and if statements
topics.description: A program can choose what to do by testing a condition.

lesson.title: Make decisions with comparisons and if statements
objectives: Compare values using common comparison operators.
Write an `if`/`elif`/`else` decision with correct indentation.
Use Boolean conditions to choose an appropriate output.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A program can choose what to do by testing a condition. Comparisons such as `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=` produce a Boolean value: `True` or `False`. An `if` statement runs its indented block when the condition is true. Use `elif` for another condition and `else` for the remaining case. Python uses indentation to show which instructions belong to each branch, so keep the indentation consistent. A single equals sign assigns a value; two equals signs compare values. Conditions can be combined with `and`, `or`, and `not`, but a beginner should first make each individual comparison clear. Test boundary values: if a pass mark is 50, check 49, 50, and 51. A well-chosen boundary test can reveal an incorrect `<` where `<=` was intended. The sample below classifies a practice score only; it does not report a real learner result.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The comparison `score >= 50` evaluates to `True` for 55, so Python runs the first indented block and skips `else`. With a score of 49, the condition would be false and the second message would be displayed.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A condition branches to one indented block when true and to an alternative block when false.
blocks.content: condition true?  → yes: run if block  |  no: run else block

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Write a practice program that asks for a whole-number temperature and prints `warm` when it is at least 20, otherwise prints `cool`. Test 19, 20, and 21; then add a separate `hot` case at 30 or above.
success_checks: The comparisons use the correct boundary operators.
Each branch is indented consistently.
The three boundary values take the expected branches.

items.prompt: What does `==` do?
If `score` is 50, what is the result of `score >= 50`?
Which rule shows the body of an `if` statement in Python?

choices.text: It is enclosed in curly braces
It is indented beneath the condition
It must be on a comment line
It is placed before the condition

revision_notes: Comparisons produce `True` or `False`.
Use `if`, optional `elif`, and optional `else` for choices.
Check boundary cases and remember `=` assigns while `==` compares.

modules.title: Repeat work and organize reusable data
modules.description: Use loops, ordered lists, and functions to make programs that can handle repeated information.

topics.title: Repeat instructions with for and while loops
topics.description: A loop repeats a block of instructions.

lesson.title: Repeat instructions with for and while loops
objectives: Choose a `for` loop for a known sequence of values.
Explain the stopping behavior of `range()`.
Use a `while` loop with a condition that can eventually become false.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A loop repeats a block of instructions. Use a `for` loop when you want to visit each value in a known sequence, such as each title in a list. `range(start, stop)` produces integers starting at `start` and stopping just before `stop`; the stop number is not included. For example, `range(1, 4)` visits 1, 2, and 3. A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true. The program must update something used in the condition, or it may never stop. Choose the loop that makes the intended repetition easiest to read. Indent the repeated block consistently. When practicing, count how many times the body should run before executing the code, then compare your prediction with the output. A loop is not a shortcut for unclear instructions: it is a precise way to express a repeated action.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
for number in range(1, 4):
    print(number)

countdown = 3
while countdown > 0:
    print(countdown)
    countdown = countdown - 1
print("Go!")
blocks.explanation: The `for` loop visits three values because 4 is excluded. The `while` loop starts with 3 and subtracts 1 on each pass; eventually the condition `countdown > 0` is false, so the loop ends before `Go!` prints.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A loop checks its condition, runs a body, advances or updates, then checks again until it stops.
blocks.content: check loop condition  →  run indented body  →  update/reach next value  →  check again

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Use a `for` loop to display each number from 1 through 5. Then use a `while` loop to count from 3 down to 1. Before running, write down the expected number of repetitions and identify what makes the while condition stop being true.
success_checks: The for-loop range includes 5 by using a stop value of 6.
The countdown updates on every pass.
Both loops terminate and display the predicted number of values.

items.prompt: How many values are produced by `range(2, 5)`?
Which loop is often clearest for visiting every item in a list?
What is a common cause of an unintended infinite `while` loop?

choices.text: The loop condition can never be true
The loop body never updates a value needed to make the condition false
The variable has a descriptive name

revision_notes: Use `for` to visit a known sequence and `while` to repeat while a condition holds.
`range` includes its start and excludes its stop value.
Update a while-loop condition so it can eventually become false.

topics.title: Keep ordered data in lists
topics.description: A list stores an ordered collection of values.

lesson.title: Keep ordered data in lists
objectives: Create a list and access an item by its zero-based index.
Add an item with `append()` and inspect a list's length.
Use a loop to process each item in a list.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A list stores an ordered collection of values. Square brackets create a list, and commas separate its items. Python counts positions from zero: the first item has index 0, the second index 1, and so on. `titles[1]` therefore reads the second title, not the first. `append(value)` adds one new item to the end, and `len(titles)` returns the number of items. A `for` loop can visit every item without requiring the learner to calculate each index. Lists are useful when several related values need the same kind of treatment. Indexing past the final item causes an `IndexError`, so check a list's length or loop directly over it. This example keeps a few fictional book titles in memory; when the program ends, the list disappears because file storage is outside this course.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
titles = ["Mti wa Hadithi", "Safari ya Mwezi"]
titles.append("Sauti za Mto")
print(titles[1])
print(len(titles))
for title in titles:
    print(title)
blocks.expected_output:
Safari ya Mwezi
3
Mti wa Hadithi
Safari ya Mwezi
Sauti za Mto
blocks.explanation: Appending adds the third title. Index 1 selects the second item, and `len` reports three items. The `for` loop then displays each title in its original order.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A three-item list with indices 0, 1, and 2 shows that Python's first list position is zero.
blocks.content:
index:     0                 1                    2
value:  Mti wa Hadithi | Safari ya Mwezi | Sauti za Mto

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Create a list of three fictional book titles. Print the first item, append a fourth, print the length, then loop over the list to display every title. Predict the index of the third title before running the program.
success_checks: The third title uses index 2.
After appending one value, the list length is four.
The for loop prints each title once and in order.

items.prompt: What index refers to the first item in a Python list?
What does `items.append("new")` do?

choices.text: Adds the value to the end of the list

items.prompt: How can a program display each value in a list once?

choices.text: Use a `for` loop over the list

revision_notes: Lists preserve order and use square brackets.
Indexes start at zero; `append()` adds to the end and `len()` counts items.
A `for` loop is a clear way to process every list item.

topics.title: Reuse steps with functions
topics.description: A function is a named group of instructions that can be called when needed.

lesson.title: Reuse steps with functions
objectives: Define and call a function with `def`.
Pass an argument and return a calculated result.
Distinguish a returned value from text printed by a function.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A function is a named group of instructions that can be called when needed. Define one with `def`, a function name, parentheses, and a colon. The indented body contains its steps. A parameter is a name in the function definition that receives a value; an argument is the value supplied in a call. `return` sends a result back to the caller, while `print` displays something for a person. A function can calculate and return without printing, which makes its result reusable in another calculation. Keep a function focused on one clear job. The example below converts minutes to seconds. After defining a function, nothing inside its body runs until the function is called. Calling it with different arguments lets the same instructions work with different data. Descriptive function names normally use lowercase words separated by underscores.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
def minutes_to_seconds(minutes):
    return minutes * 60

first_total = minutes_to_seconds(2)
print(first_total)
print(minutes_to_seconds(5))
blocks.explanation: `minutes` is the parameter. The calls pass 2 and 5 as arguments. The function returns each multiplication result, and `print` displays those returned values. The function itself does not print anything.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A function call supplies an argument, the function uses its parameter, and a returned value goes back to the caller.
blocks.content: call with argument  →  function body uses parameter  →  return value to caller

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Write a function named `double_value` that accepts a number and returns twice that number. Call it with 4 and 9. Store one result in a variable, then print both results outside the function.
success_checks: The function body is indented beneath `def`.
The result is sent back with `return`.
Calls with 4 and 9 display 8 and 18.

items.prompt: What does `return` do in a function?

choices.text: Sends a result back to the caller

items.prompt: In `def double(n):`, what is `n`?
What is printed by `def double(n): return n * 2` followed by `print(double(4))`?

revision_notes: Define a reusable function with `def` and call it by name.
Parameters receive arguments; `return` sends a value back.
Printing displays output, while returning makes a value available to other code.

modules.title: Combine structures and build confidently
modules.description: Represent labelled records, handle common errors, test behavior, and combine the fundamentals in a small program.

topics.title: Group labelled information in dictionaries
topics.description: A dictionary stores related values under keys.

lesson.title: Group labelled information in dictionaries
objectives: Create a dictionary that maps keys to values.
Read and update a value using its key.
Use a list of dictionaries for a small collection of records.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A dictionary stores related values under keys. Curly braces contain key-value pairs separated by commas; a colon separates each key from its value. A key such as `"title"` labels the value it belongs to. Read a value with square brackets, for example `book["title"]`. A dictionary can hold different types, such as a string title and a Boolean availability flag. Assigning to an existing key updates that value. A list of dictionaries can represent several similar records, and a loop can visit each record. Keys must be used consistently; asking for a missing key with square brackets raises a `KeyError`. The course project uses dictionaries to represent books, but it deliberately does not store a learner's name or track who borrows an item. This simple structure is for a small in-memory practice program, not a secure library database.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
book = {"title": "Mti wa Hadithi", "available": True}
print(book["title"])
book["available"] = False
print(book["available"])
books = [book, {"title": "Safari ya Mwezi", "available": True}]
print(len(books))
blocks.explanation: The dictionary maps `title` to text and `available` to a Boolean. The assignment changes only the availability value. The list then contains two dictionary records, which can be processed with a loop.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A dictionary record maps descriptive keys to values, and a list can group multiple such records.
blocks.content:
book record: { title → text, available → True/False }
collection: [book record, book record, ...]

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Create a dictionary for one fictional book with `title` and `available` keys. Print both values, change availability, and place the record in a list. Loop over the list and display each title.
success_checks: The dictionary keys are quoted strings and consistently spelled.
The availability value is Boolean, not the text `"True"`.
The list loop reads the title from each dictionary.

items.prompt: How do you read the title from `book = {"title": "Mti"}`?
Which value is a Boolean availability flag?
What does `book["available"] = False` do when that key exists?

choices.text: Updates the value for that key

revision_notes: Dictionaries map keys to values and use curly braces.
Read or update a value through its key in square brackets.
A list of dictionaries can represent multiple similar records.

topics.title: Read errors, validate input, and test small pieces
topics.description: Errors are clues about what the program could not do.

lesson.title: Read errors, validate input, and test small pieces
objectives: Distinguish a syntax error from a runtime error.
Handle a possible number-conversion error with `try` and `except`.
Test a function using representative examples and `assert`.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Errors are clues about what the program could not do. A syntax error means Python could not understand the code's structure, such as a missing colon. A runtime error happens while valid-looking code runs, such as converting the word `five` to an integer. A traceback names the error type and often points to the line that caused it. Use `try` around an operation that may fail, and catch the specific exception you expect with `except ValueError`. Give a calm, useful message and let the program ask again or stop safely. Do not hide every error with a broad catch-all; unexpected problems should remain visible while learning. Small functions can be checked with known inputs and expected outputs. Python's `assert condition` raises `AssertionError` when a condition is false and does nothing when it is true. These checks help during practice; they are not a complete replacement for careful review.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: Valid digits return an integer. The specific `ValueError` handler returns `None` for text that cannot be converted. The two assertions check one valid and one invalid case; if either expected result is wrong, Python raises an assertion error before printing the final message.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A conversion either returns the number or follows a ValueError path to a safe fallback.
blocks.content:
try conversion  →  succeeds: return number
               ↘ ValueError: return a safe fallback

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Write a function that converts text to an integer and returns `None` when conversion fails. Test `"7"`, `"0"`, and `"seven"` with assertions. Add one clear message in a small caller for the invalid case.
success_checks: Only `ValueError` is handled for the conversion.
Valid numeric text returns an integer and invalid text returns `None`.
All three examples are checked with expected outcomes.

items.prompt: What error can `int("five")` raise?
What happens when an `assert` condition is true?

choices.text: The assertion passes without raising an error

items.prompt: Why is catching only `ValueError` often better than catching every error?

choices.text: It handles the expected conversion problem without hiding unrelated bugs
It guarantees there are no bugs
It removes the need for testing

Use `try`/`except ValueError` around a conversion that may fail.
Test representative valid and invalid inputs with expected results.

topics.title: Combine Python fundamentals in a small program
topics.description: A complete beginner program brings familiar pieces together.

lesson.title: Combine Python fundamentals in a small program
objectives: Combine lists, dictionaries, functions, decisions, and loops in one program.
Trace a simple program from input through processing to output.
Use a short test checklist to verify normal and edge cases.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A complete beginner program brings familiar pieces together. Use a list to hold several book dictionaries, functions to name each operation, loops to display or search records, and conditions to choose an action. Start by describing what the program should do in plain language, then identify its data and the sequence of steps. Build one small behavior at a time and run it with a few examples. Test a normal case, an empty input, a value that is not found, and an invalid menu choice. The example combines a loop, a list, dictionaries, a function, a decision, and a safe search that rejects a blank phrase. It keeps its data in memory only. The practical project later extends this idea with adding and updating books. There is no network, login, permanent storage, or personal borrower data. Keep the goal small enough that you can explain each line and predict what it will do.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The function normalizes the search text and returns `None` immediately when the cleaned phrase is empty. Otherwise it loops through records and returns the first matching dictionary. The `if` statement checks whether a match was found before reading its title; a missing title also returns `None` and uses the alternative message.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A search request moves through a function that checks a collection, then a condition selects a found or not-found message.
blocks.content: question/input  →  function + collection search  →  condition checks result  →  clear message

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Run the search example for `mti`, `mwezi`, and `ocean`. Change the records and predict each result. Then write a short test checklist with one found title, one missing title, and an empty search. Explain which Python construct handles each step.
success_checks: A matching title is reported without an error.
A missing title returns `None` and uses the alternative branch.
The learner identifies the function, loop, dictionary, and conditional in the program.

items.prompt: Why does `find_title` return `None` after its loop when no title matches?

choices.text: It signals that no record was found
It means the list was sorted
It changes the title to lowercase

items.prompt: Which is a useful edge case for a title-search function?

choices.text: Only a title that definitely exists
An empty search phrase and a phrase that is not found

items.prompt: Which set best describes the example's main Python structures?

choices.text: List, dictionaries, function, loop, and conditional
Only a comment and a string
A database and a network server
A class and an imported package

blocks.title: School Library Reading-List Helper
blocks.purpose: Build a small, in-memory Python program that helps a class browse a fictional set of library book titles and their availability. Focus on programming fundamentals, not on building a deployed library system.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional book titles only; do not collect learner names, borrower names, contact details, or student identifiers.
Keep data in memory for one run. The program does not save files, contact a network, or provide accounts.
Use only Python 3.10+ and the standard library.
requirements: Start with at least three fictional book dictionaries containing a title and Boolean availability value.
Show all titles and clearly indicate whether each is available.
Allow a user to add a title; trim outer spaces and reject a blank or case-insensitive duplicate.
Allow a case-insensitive partial-title search and show a helpful message if no result is found.
Allow a title's availability to be changed to borrowed or returned; do not store who borrowed it.
Use at least three small functions, a list, dictionaries, a loop, and conditional decisions.
Handle an unknown menu choice without crashing and provide a clear exit option.
suggested_steps: Create a list of book dictionaries and print it in a readable form.
Write and test one function to add a title and one to search titles.
Write a function that changes a matching book's availability.
Add a menu loop that calls the functions and exits when requested.
Test a normal case, a blank title, a duplicate, no search match, and an invalid menu choice.
success_checks: Three sample titles display correctly before and after an operation.
Blank and duplicate additions do not change the collection.
Search ignores letter case and reports a missing result safely.
Availability changes are visible, with no borrower identity recorded.
The menu can repeat and then exit; invalid choices do not stop the program unexpectedly.

rubric.look_for: List of dictionaries, display, add, search, and availability change all behave as described.
At least three focused functions and a readable menu/loop.
Appropriate if/else conditions, loops, and dictionary keys are used correctly.
Blank/duplicate input, missing searches, and invalid choices are handled calmly.
The learner demonstrates test cases, explains the code, and stores no personal borrower data.

blocks.instructions: Answer all 12 multiple-choice questions (4 marks each). Then complete both short coding tasks (26 marks each). Total: 100 marks. Use Python 3.10+ and standard-library features covered in the course. Write readable code and include at least one example test for each task.

coding_tasks.prompt: Write `classify_temperature(celsius)` that returns `"hot"` for 30 or above, `"warm"` for 20 through 29, and `"cool"` below 20. Include checks for 19, 20, 29, and 30.

coding_tasks.title: Count even numbers
coding_tasks.prompt: Write `count_even(numbers)` that returns the number of even integers in a list. Use a loop and a conditional. Include checks for `[2, 3, 4]`, an empty list, and `[1, 5]`.

revision_notes: Combine small, understandable pieces rather than writing one unexplained block.
Test normal, missing, empty, and invalid cases.
Be able to trace how inputs become processing steps and output.
